en: The V5C paper that records the vehicle’s details and its registered keeper.
Optional green ‘P’ plates some new drivers display to show they are newly qualified.
Legal cover for using a motor vehicle on public roads, protecting against claims from others at minimum.
Who legally owns the vehicle; changes of ownership must be recorded with the DVLA.
The V5C paper that records the vehicle’s details and its registered keeper.
The person named on the vehicle’s registration document as responsible for it (not always the owner).
The date when the current MOT certificate runs out and a new test is needed.
Another name for the V5C registration document showing vehicle and keeper details.
On a UK multi-lane motorway, the lane furthest to the right, normally for overtaking.
A motorway with three lanes in each direction of travel.
A speed limit you must obey by law, often shown in a red circle or on overhead gantry signs.
A person riding a bicycle on the road.
Pulling a trailer, caravan, or another vehicle behind your car using a tow bar or hitch.
Door mirrors on longer arms so you can still see past a wide trailer or caravan.
Water thrown up by tyres on a wet road that reduces how far you can see.
Devices that restrict how fast a large vehicle can go, often required by law for lorries.
A braking system on many large vehicles that uses compressed air instead of only hydraulic fluid.
When a vehicle starts moving off from a stop, such as leaving a bus stop.
Tall vehicles such as lorries or vans that can be pushed sideways by strong wind.
The downward weight a trailer’s hitch puts on the vehicle’s tow ball; it must stay within limits.
The metal bar fitted to a vehicle for attaching and towing a trailer or caravan.
A safety device that holds a child securely in the vehicle, such as a child seat.
A seat belt that goes only across the hips, without a diagonal shoulder strap.
An unpowered wheeled unit designed to be towed behind a vehicle to carry loads.
Extra or extended side mirrors required when a trailer is wider than the towing vehicle.
Flags or lights that mark an overhanging load so other road users can see it.
A small wheel near the trailer hitch used to support and manoeuvre the trailer when unhitched.
Support legs at the corners of a caravan used to keep it stable when parked, not while towing.
A device that reduces unwanted swinging or swaying of a trailer while towing.
Carrying more weight than the vehicle or trailer is legally allowed to carry.
The official body that issues and manages driving licences and related vehicle records (e.g. DVLA).
A trailer without its own brakes; coupling safety devices are especially important.
A backup link (often a chain or cable) that keeps the trailer attached if the main coupling fails.
The ball-shaped coupling on a tow bar that the trailer hitch locks onto.
How the car steers, corners, and responds; a heavy load can make this worse.
Optional plates some newly qualified drivers display to show they have just passed their test.
The heaviest legal weight of a vehicle or trailer including its load (also called MAM).
Side-to-side swinging of a trailer or caravan while being towed, which can become dangerous.
The pedal that increases engine power and vehicle speed (also called the gas pedal).
Using the vehicle horn to make a warning sound.
Raised sections across the road designed to slow traffic down.
A rule that limits or bans motorcycles on that stretch of road.
Vehicles built mainly to carry cargo rather than passengers.
Turning the vehicle around in a U-shape to go back the way you came.
A painted zone with diagonal stripes that separates traffic streams.
Dashed white road markings, often showing a boundary you may cross when safe.
A road where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
A camera that records vehicles breaking the speed limit.
A stretch where cameras measure your average speed between two points.
A road where traffic is allowed to travel in only one direction.
A road without a central reservation separating opposite directions of traffic.
A path that pedestrians and cyclists may both use.
The right to go first when roads meet or when rules give you precedence.
Vehicles that have stopped and are not moving, often in a queue.
A metric unit of weight used on UK restriction signs for heavy vehicles.
Dangerous substances such as chemicals or fuel that need special care in transport.
Rest areas on a motorway with fuel, food, and toilets.
The road becoming less wide ahead.
Places of interest for visitors, such as landmarks or museums.
A temporary alternative path around a closed or blocked road.
A sharp slope going downwards where speed can increase quickly.
A section of road going up a slope.
A metric unit of length used on UK height and width restriction signs.
A bridge with a sharp rise in the middle that can hide traffic beyond it.
Large goods vehicles used to carry freight (UK term for trucks).
Planes flying near the ground, often near an airport approach.
Air above an area where flying is limited or controlled for safety.
A part of the road reserved for cyclists, often marked with a bicycle symbol.
An order you must follow, not just advice.
A rule that forbids a particular action or type of vehicle.
An order you must follow, not just advice.
A limit on what you may do, such as speed, access, or vehicle type.
Rules you are legally required to obey.
The more important road at a junction, which usually has priority.
Short-term construction or repairs that change normal road conditions.
An area where cameras check your average speed over a stretch of road.
Short-term alternative routes when the normal road is closed or blocked.
Say or show the opposite of something else.
A short post on the road used to mark an island, edge, or obstruction.
Road features designed to slow vehicles down, such as humps or narrowings.
